underground_reservoir: A giant storage tunnel dug beneath a main road. During heavy rain it swallows the excess stormwater and holds it, then slowly releases it after the storm — so the streets above never flood. Needs no surface land, which is why Tokyo builds it under dense districts.
mega_discharge_channel: The world's largest storm drain: colossal underground tanks and tunnels that catch overflow from several rivers at once and pump it to a big river after the peak. A decade-long megaproject for the worst, repeatedly-flooded areas.
multipurpose_retention_basin: A large low park or sports ground deliberately allowed to flood during storms — holding water like a temporary lake — then drained and reused as a park in dry weather. Turns open public land into flood storage.
schoolyard_park_storage: A cheap mini retention basin: school grounds and parks are graded to hold a shallow layer of rainwater for a few hours, shaving the peak off local flooding. Fast, using land the city already owns.
building_rainwater_storage: A city rule that every new building stores its own rainwater in a tank and releases it slowly. Thousands of small tanks across a dense area add up to major flood storage with no big construction.
permeable_pavement: Porous road and footpath surfaces that let rainwater soak into the ground instead of rushing into drains — cutting the water that ever reaches the drainage system. Retrofitted when roads are resurfaced.
infiltration_inlets: Roadside pits and planted rain gardens that catch runoff and let it seep into the soil. Cheap, small, scattered across residential streets to reduce mild flooding.
super_levee: A very wide, gently sloping riverbank — hundreds of metres across — that water cannot overtop or breach like a normal narrow flood wall. Its top is usable land. Protects riverfront districts from the river bursting.
river_widening: Physically widening and deepening the river channel so it carries far more water before spilling into the city. A direct fix where the river's capacity is the bottleneck.
sabo_check_dam: Small stepped barriers across steep upstream streams that trap debris and slow fast torrents before they reach the city. Japan's signature erosion-control export; only useful on steep terrain.
hazard_maps: Official flood-risk maps every neighbourhood must publish, showing which areas flood and where to evacuate. It doesn't stop flooding but saves lives and guides investment — a near-zero-cost first step.
xrain_radar: A dense weather-radar network predicting rainfall street-by-street, minute-by-minute, so the city gets early warning and can operate pumps and gates ahead of the flood. Warning, not prevention.
basin_flood_management: Managing the whole river basin as one system — coordinating storage, land use and forecasting across every town and agency along the river, instead of each area defending itself alone.
comprehensive_flood_control: Combines hard construction with land-use rules and on-site storage across a fast-growing city — the exact framework Japan's JICA used to build Chennai's flood master plan, directly relevant to Indian cities.
